S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a written incident report with known causes and affected units within 10 days. They shall notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential hazard relevant to their units, with clear safety instructions and support.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, or injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a written incident report with known causes and affected units within 10 days. They shall notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential hazard relevant to their units, with clear safety instructions and support. Reports shall include incidents regardless of whether injury or property damage occurred.

parameters.quote: The maximum allowed failure rate shall be 5% of tested units. S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: The maximum allowed failure rate shall be 5% of tested units. Manufacturers shall submit per-model protocols, sample sizes, failure rates, and corrective actions to regulators, and shall provide the per-model failure rate and relevant test information to customers purchasing that model. For models already marketed when this standard is adopted, the regulator may authorize a time-limited transition period with interim safeguards and milestones before restricting sales, based on the evidence and severity of risk.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. The maximum allowed failure rate shall be 5% of tested units. Manufacturers shall submit per-model protocols, sample sizes, failure rates, and corrective actions to regulators, and shall provide the per-model failure rate and relevant test information to customers purchasing that model. Per-model failure rates shall not be published to the general public. A model exceeding 5% shall have a regulator-supervised corrective-action plan and retest schedule. For models already marketed when this standard is adopted, the regulator may authorize a time-limited transition period with interim safeguards and milestones before restricting sales, based on the evidence and severity of risk.

parameters.quote: New home battery units shall provide a secure remote emergency shut-off function beginning on adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units that lack this function within six years of adoption, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved emergency isolation measure.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery units shall provide a secure remote emergency shut-off function beginning on adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units that lack this function within six years of adoption, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved emergency isolation measure.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery units shall provide a secure remote emergency shut-off function beginning on adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall retrofit installed units that lack this function within six years of adoption, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved emergency isolation measure. The function shall be accessible to authorized emergency responders and customers, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions.

parameters.quote: All new home battery units shall include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: All new home battery units shall include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new home battery units shall include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall document suppression-system performance and maintenance requirements in customer materials.

parameters.quote: A mandatory recall is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year, or when the regulator determines a defect presents an unreasonable serious safety risk. Manufacturers shall report the underlying model-level data to regulators and notify affected customers without undue delay; notices must explain the hazard, affected units, and remedy.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A mandatory recall is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year, or when the regulator determines a defect presents an unreasonable serious safety risk. Manufacturers shall report the underlying model-level data to regulators and notify affected customers without undue delay; notices must explain the hazard, affected units, and remedy.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers shall promptly notify affected customers of incidents or defects that could create a fire, overheating, or injury hazard, with clear instructions for safe use and support. A mandatory recall is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a rolling year, or when the regulator determines a defect presents an unreasonable serious safety risk. Manufacturers shall report the underlying model-level data to regulators and notify affected customers without undue delay; notices must explain the hazard, affected units, and remedy.

judge_section_notes: S2 keeps the 5% limit but removes any mandatory sales stop for models above it, and the transition for already-marketed models has no fixed end, so it is weakened in practice; the 7% cap was dropped. S5 sets a mandatory 8-per-100k recall with no transition, which would immediately affect Halcyon's Ember 8 at 9.9, while S3's six-year retrofit favours Northwind's 38% shut-off coverage. S4 is set at 36 months, the earliest date Halcyon's red line permitted.
